I'll start by fixing the interpretation: fluid = disc (r≤58, z 4→18) + inlet annulus (r 12→16, z 18→22), minus the hub cylinder (r 12) and minus 7 backward-curved blades. All in metres from the start.

```python
import numpy as np, os, subprocess
from build123d import *

mm = 1e-3
R_BP, T_BP = 60*mm, 4*mm          # backplate (reference only)
R_HUB, H_HUB = 12*mm, 18*mm       # hub rises 18 mm from backplate top
Z0 = T_BP                          # backplate top surface, z = 4 mm
Z_SHR = Z0 + 14*mm                 # shroud, 14 mm above backplate  -> 18 mm
Z_TOP = Z0 + H_HUB                 # hub top / inlet plane -> 22 mm
R1, R2 = 16*mm, 58*mm              # blade leading / trailing radius
T_BL, N_BL = 3*mm, 7               # blade thickness, count
WRAP = np.radians(30.0)            # backward sweep, against rotation

def camber(n=60):
    r = np.linspace(R1, R2, n)
    th = -WRAP*(r-R1)/(R2-R1)      # negative = backward (against +theta rotation)
    return r, th

r, th = camber()
print("wrap deg =", np.degrees(th[0]-th[-1]), " r1,r2 mm =", r[0]/mm, r[-1]/mm)
print("pitch at R1 (mm) =", 2*np.pi*R1/N_BL/mm, " passage gap =", (2*np.pi*R1/N_BL-T_BL)/mm)
```
I'll set up the parameters and check the blade pitch before building anything.

Narrowest passage is 11.4 mm, so cells around 1.2–1.5 mm. A 2 mm root fillet would need ~0.4 mm cells to survive snapping — I'll drop the fillets and say so. Now the blade solid: camber offset ±1.5 mm, extruded full height, extended past r=58 so the outlet cylinder trims it cleanly.
The extrude went in −Z; I'll place it explicitly rather than rely on the face normal.
Now the fluid volume: the impeller disc plus the axial eye annulus, minus hub and blades.
Fluid is a single solid. Now classify faces by their actual surface geometry (plane z, cylinder axis/radius) — not bounding box — and count each group.
Group areas match the analytic annuli (inlet π(16²−12²)=351.9, hub 2π·12·18=1357.2). Now measure the blade wrap angle and thickness from the built solid itself.
The wrap measurement was biased by which flank vertices got caught. Measuring the camber line properly, as the midpoint of the two flank points at each end.
Let me measure camber angle as the mid of the two flanks within radius bands, which doesn't depend on vertex ordering.
Wrap is 29.8° backward, thickness 3.0 mm, height 14 mm. Now export each named group to its own STL and render the fluid volume to look at it.
Shape is right. Now the coarsest mesh that exists: blockMesh box + snappyHexMesh with the six STL regions as named patches.
Mesh OK, volume 129309 mm³ vs CAD 129330 mm³ (0.02%). The inlet annulus only has 148 faces though, so refine: 2 mm base with level 1 on all surfaces (~1 mm at walls, 4 cells across the eye).
84k cells, Mesh OK, volume within 0.007% of CAD. Let me look at the mesh patches.
Mesh looks right: 7 backward-curved passages, green inlet annulus at the eye, orange hub, purple radial outlet.
Free edges and self-intersections in the STLs. Let me find which patch file is at fault.
Every file reports nearly all edges open — the triangles aren't sharing vertices. Let me look at what was actually written.
Binary STL in float32 — the quantization stops shared vertices from welding. I'll re-export in full-precision ASCII from the tessellation directly.
Per-face tessellation doesn't share edge nodes. I'll mesh the whole solid once with BRepMesh so adjacent faces share their edge polygons, then read each face's triangulation.
Volume is right but 2177 free edges persist — let me see where they are.
Free edges sit entirely on the two annuli at r 12–16. Let me look at them.
Three seam circles (r=12 and 16 at the inlet plane, r=12 at the backplate) have duplicate/unshared edges from the booleans. Let me clean the solid's redundant topology and re-tessellate.
